summary: Extends Mobile IP to support reverse tunnels, where traffic from a mobile node is sent back through its home agent. This keeps packets topologically correct when networks filter based on source addresses. It does not try to solve firewall problems. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: If your mail must come from your home address, you send it back home first so it can be sent out properly. This lets a roaming device do the same for its Internet traffic.

subtitle: How a roaming Mobile IP device sends its traffic back through its home agent so source addresses stay topologically correct.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP assumes routers forward packets by destination address only, but routers that check source addresses are increasingly common, and a roaming node's packets carry its home address as source, which does not match the network it is on.
tldr.mechanism: A new T bit in agent advertisements and Registration Requests lets a mobile node ask for a reverse tunnel from its care-of address to its home agent, with packets reaching the foreign agent in either the Direct or the Encapsulating Delivery Style.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3024 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2344. It makes the Encapsulating Delivery Style optional (SHOULD), adds new reply code 79 and adds an appendix on disparate address spaces.

facts.label: New flag
facts.value: T bit, in advertisements and Registration Requests

today: RFC 3024 is a Proposed Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2344, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Reverse Tunnels
sections.content:
The Mobile IP specification assumes that IP unicast datagrams are routed by destination address, not by source address. Because of security concerns such as IP spoofing, routers that break this assumption are, in the RFC's words, increasingly common. Such routers need both the source and destination address of a packet to be topologically correct.

The forward tunnel already is: its endpoints are the home agent address and the care-of address, both properly assigned where they sit. But a packet sent by the mobile node has its home address as source, which does not match the network prefix it is sent from.

The fix is a reverse tunnel that starts at the care-of address and ends at the home agent. The RFC lists other uses of reverse tunnels too: mobile routers, joining and sending to multicast groups in the home network, and packets whose TTL is so low they would expire on the way home, since the tunnel counts as one decrement.

The RFC assumes a common IP address space, no intervening firewalls (or firewalls that share the needed security association), and symmetric tunnels that use the same configuration as the forward tunnel, with IP in IP encapsulation unless stated otherwise. It is aimed mainly at mobile nodes that rely on a foreign agent for forward tunnel support.
sections.eli5: Some gatekeepers only let a letter through if the return address matches where it was mailed from. A traveler's letters say 'home' but are mailed from far away, so they get stopped. Sending them home first fixes that.

sections.title: How It Works in Brief
sections.content:
A mobile node arrives on a foreign network, listens to agent advertisements and picks a foreign agent that offers reverse tunneling. It asks for the service when it registers through that agent, and it also says how it will hand packets to the foreign agent.

There are two choices. In the Direct Delivery Style the mobile node makes the foreign agent its default router and sends plain, unencapsulated packets; the foreign agent intercepts them and tunnels them to the home agent. In the Encapsulating Delivery Style the mobile node encapsulates every outgoing packet to the foreign agent, which decapsulates and re-tunnels it to the home agent, using its own care-of address as the entry point of the new tunnel.
sections.eli5: You can drop your letter straight into the hotel's outgoing box, or you can seal it in an extra envelope addressed to the hotel desk. Either way, the hotel then forwards it home.

sections.title: New Bits, Extension and Reply Codes
sections.content:
The RFC adds one flag, the T bit, in two places. In the Mobility Agent Advertisement Extension it means the agent offers reverse tunneling service; a foreign agent that sets it MUST support the Direct Delivery Style and SHOULD support the Encapsulating one. A mobile node that does not understand the bit ignores it. In the Registration Request it uses one of the reserved bits and means the node asks its home agent to accept a reverse tunnel from the care-of address (or, with a foreign agent care-of address, asks the foreign agent to reverse-tunnel its packets).

A mobile node MAY also include an Encapsulating Delivery Style Extension. It is a two-field extension with Type 130 and Length 0. The foreign agent MUST consume it rather than relay it, it MUST NOT be present unless T is set, and if it is absent Direct Delivery is assumed.

New Registration Reply codes report failures. Foreign agents can deny with 74, 75, 76 or 79, and home agents with 137, 138 or 139. A mobile node must still accept the older codes 70 and 134 (poorly formed request) in reply to a request with T set, but agents that support reverse tunneling MUST use 74 and 137.
sections.eli5: The new feature is one extra checkbox on the registration form that says 'please send my mail back home'. There are also a few new 'no, because...' messages for when the answer is no.

sections.title: What Each Party Does
sections.content:
Unless stated otherwise, ordinary Mobile IP behavior applies, including the use of authentication extensions between parties that share a mobility security association. An admissible authentication extension MUST always be present between a mobile node and its home agent.

The mobile node sets T and MUST set the IP TTL of the Registration Request to 255. If the request is denied, it MAY retry with fewer requests, or even with T cleared, though in that case data transfer may not be possible. On success with a foreign agent care-of address it MUST use the delivery style it asked for.

The foreign agent processes the request as usual, then MUST verify that the TTL is 255 and otherwise reject with code 76, sending such replies at most once per second. It returns 72 for an unsupported encapsulation, 79 for an unsupported delivery style and 74 if it cannot support a matching reverse tunnel. Otherwise it relays the request, and on a valid reply records in its visitor list that the node has a reverse tunnel and its delivery style.

The home agent returns 139 for an unsupported encapsulation and 137 if it cannot support a matching reverse tunnel, and records the grant in its mobility bindings. It MUST implement, and by default SHOULD enable, a check on encapsulated packets addressed to itself: it looks for a binding whose care-of address is the outer source and whose mobile node address is the inner source. With no match, or with a mechanism not negotiated, it MUST silently discard the packet and SHOULD log a security exception. Valid packets are decapsulated and forwarded to the correspondent host.
sections.eli5: Each helper has a checklist. The traveler asks, the hotel desk checks the request really came from the same building, and the home office only forwards mail it expects. Anything that does not match is quietly thrown away.

sections.title: Delivery Styles and Packet Headers
sections.content:
In the Direct Delivery Style the mobile node sends an ordinary packet (source: its home address, destination: the correspondent host) to the foreign agent, which MUST be its default router. This is simple and keeps packets small on a possibly slow link, but it supports only unicast and no selective reverse tunneling. The foreign agent adds an outer header: source copied from the Care-of Address field of the Registration Request, destination copied from the Home Agent field of the most recent successful Registration Reply, and protocol 4 (IP in IP) unless another method was negotiated.

In the Encapsulating Delivery Style the mobile node builds the outer header itself, with its home address as source and the foreign agent's address as destination. The foreign agent verifies the sender, decapsulates, and re-encapsulates toward the home agent. An unencapsulated packet from a node that asked for this style MUST NOT be reverse tunneled and is forwarded by normal IP routing.

Mobile nodes that want to send broadcast or multicast through a foreign agent MUST use the Encapsulating style. Nodes with a co-located care-of address follow the usual Mobile IP rules instead. Selective reverse tunneling lets a node skip the tunnel for local resources such as a nearby printer: packets sent Direct are forwarded normally, and packets sent Encapsulated MUST be reverse tunneled.
sections.eli5: You can hand the hotel an open postcard it will re-wrap for you, or wrap it yourself first. Wrapping it yourself also lets you decide which cards go home and which stay in town.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions inherit the security considerations of the Mobile IP specification, and creating both forward and reverse tunnels involves authentication. The main worry is hijacking: a malicious node could inject packets into a tunnel, and since packets leave the tunnel exit toward the wider network, reverse tunnels can make this worse. An unauthenticated exchange with the foreign agent could also let an attacker redirect an existing reverse tunnel to another home agent.

The best protection is the Mobile-Foreign and Foreign-Home Authentication Extensions. Without the needed security associations, the TTL of 255 on Registration Requests keeps nodes more than one hop away from posing as valid mobile nodes, and the extra denial codes make attacks easier to track. The working group considered mechanisms based on unauthenticated state but judged the denial-of-service risk too high for only weak protection.

The RFC also addresses a worry that administrators will filter IP in IP packets: it cites the ingress filtering recommendation, which says that tracking an attack is simpler when the source is more likely to be valid. For disparate address spaces, the link layer MUST securely authenticate traffic from mobile nodes, and unauthenticated technologies such as shared ethernet are not recommended.
sections.eli5: A sneaky stranger might try to use your tunnel to send mail pretending to be you. Checking IDs and only accepting requests from right next door makes that much harder.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: The Encapsulating Delivery Style extension is a Mobile IP registration extension, and IANA assigned value 130 for it when RFC 2344 was published. The reply codes are Mobile IP error codes: at that time IANA assigned 74-76 for foreign agent rejections and 137-139 for home agent rejections. The code for 'delivery style not supported' has been assigned the value 79.
sections.eli5: Each new message type needs its own official number, like a locker number. These numbers were handed out so nothing clashes.

sections.title: Disparate Address Spaces
sections.content:
Appendix A, new in this revision, covers cases where the mobile node, foreign agent and home agent do not share one routable address space, for example when private addresses from RFC 1918 are in use. Reverse tunneling can help within limits: the correspondent and mobile node must not be in disparate spaces, the foreign agent and home agent must reach each other directly, and no new protocol elements are added.

When two mobile nodes visiting one foreign agent have the same numeric address, the foreign agent cannot use the home address alone. For forward tunnels it uses the inner destination address plus the outer source and destination addresses, learned at registration. For reverse tunnels it uses link-layer information (such as a MAC address, a PPP session or a device ID) plus the source IP address.

It also describes the Limited Private Address Scenario, where only mobile nodes have private addresses. There mobile nodes MUST set T, foreign agents MUST have publicly routable care-of addresses and MUST support reverse tunneling for such nodes, and home agents MUST use publicly routable addresses and MUST accept their registrations.
sections.eli5: If two kids in the same hotel have the same nickname, the desk cannot tell their mail apart by name alone. It also looks at which room each kid is in.
